Work on Linear issue ENT-1989:

Suggested branch name: pfleidi/ent-1989-explain-missing-blob-probe-lazy-fetches-per-blob-hammering

<issue identifier="ENT-1989">
<title>explain: missing-blob probe lazy-fetches per blob, hammering mirrors with bogus wants</title>
<description>
> Agent-generated issue. Verify facts against source. Treat proposed solutions, recommendations, and agent-made decisions as hypotheses, not settled direction.

Repo: `entireio/cli`

## Observed facts

* On 2026-08-26 ~21:42–22:12 UTC, `entire explain --checkpoint 01M07BGK52MB63Y83A0RVYQB2N --json` runs (invoked by a codex agent session in a local `entireio/cli` clone) produced **1,805 single-want** `git-upload-pack` **requests** against the `entire://aws-us-east-2` mirrors of `entireio/cli` and `entireio/cli-checkpoints`, all answered `503`. entiredb's shadow classifier tagged 100% of them `verdict:bogus` (objects the repos never contained). The resulting 17–38% error rate on the git-protocol route tripped the availability SLO fast burn and paged P1 ([incident.io](<http://incident.io>) INC-78, Datadog monitor 313962708-family). ap-southeast-2 was paged ~21h earlier by the same server-side class (INC-74).
* Mechanism, verified in source: `prefetchCheckpointBlobs` (`cmd/entire/cli/explain.go:902`) is designed to collect missing blobs and fetch them "in a single `git fetch-pack` invocation per store". But the collection step, `FetchingTree.CollectMissingBlobs` → `blobOnDisk` (`cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/fetching_tree.go:211`), probes each blob with a bare `git cat-file -e <hash>`. In a `blob:none` partial clone with promisor remotes, `cat-file -e` on an absent object triggers git's internal lazy fetch — one single-want upload-pack request **per configured promisor remote** — before reporting the blob missing. The batching never gets a chance.
* Each failed probe costs ~1s (remote-helper spawn + discovery per attempt, plus node failover inside the helper), so ~900 probed blobs took two ~14-minute grinds while the user-facing command sat on a spinner. Repo-local `.entire/logs/entire.log` shows the prefetch failing (`explain prefetch: cp subtree not found`, 14:46:17 and 14:56:46 -07:00) and per-file fallback reads >1s apart.
* Trigger condition: a checkpoint referenced by a commit trailer whose blobs exist only in local refs (never pushed), so every probe is a guaranteed miss on both mirrors. Any repo with the standard two entire promisor remotes doubles the requests.
* Server-side amplification (separate issue, <issue id="99c35963-dd1b-4bf4-a691-66c80401f30e" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1939/decide-whether-to-flip-the-missing-want-503-default">ENT-1939</issue>): entiredb answers never-existed wants with `503 + Retry-After: 5` instead of a terminal 40x, so these client misses count against the git-protocol availability SLO.

## Proposed approach

Set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` (or `--no-lazy-fetch`) on the `git cat-file -e` probe in `blobOnDisk` so the missing-blob analysis is a pure local check and the prefetch batches as designed. Audit the other `git cat-file` call sites in `fetching_tree.go` (`readFileViaGit`, the per-File fallback path) for the same hazard — the per-File fallback may *intentionally* fetch, but it should fetch once per blob, not probe-fetch during analysis.

## Alternatives

* Client-side negative caching / early abort after N consecutive missing-blob fetch failures in one explain run (bounds the damage but keeps the per-blob probes).
* Rely solely on the server fix (<issue id="99c35963-dd1b-4bf4-a691-66c80401f30e" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1939/decide-whether-to-flip-the-missing-want-503-default">ENT-1939</issue> terminal 40x): stops the SLO burn but keeps explain slow (~1s per missing blob) and keeps the request storm.

## Open questions

* Should the per-File fallback fetcher also stop attempting remote fetches for blobs already classified missing by the prefetch analysis in the same run?
* `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH` requires git ≥ 2.43; confirm the CLI's minimum supported git version or use `cat-file --no-lazy-fetch` / batch `cat-file --batch-check` with the env var accordingly.
</description>

Repo: `entireio/cli`

## Observed facts

* On 2026-08-26 ~21:42–22:12 UTC, `entire explain --checkpoint 01M07BGK52MB63Y83A0RVYQB2N --json` runs (invoked by a codex agent session in a local `entireio/cli` clone) produced **1,805 single-want** `git-upload-pack` **requests** against the `entire://aws-us-east-2` mirrors of `entireio/cli` and `entireio/cli-checkpoints`, all answered `503`. entiredb's shadow classifier tagged 100% of them `verdict:bogus` (objects the repos never contained). In a `blob:none` partial clone with promisor remotes, `cat-file -e` on an absent object triggers git's internal lazy fetch — one single-want upload-pack request **per configured promisor remote** — before reporting the blob missing. The batching never gets a chance.

---
name: issue-alignment
description: >
  Use when the user pastes or paraphrases a Linear issue, ticket, task, bug,
  feature request, acceptance criteria, product spec, or issue-generated prompt
  that could lead to implementation. Also use when the prompt includes issue
  IDs, acceptance criteria, "recommended approach", "do it", "come up with a
  plan", asks to start work from a tracker item, or asks how to validate an
  issue is complete after deploy.
---

# Issue Alignment

Use this skill before planning or implementing work that starts from an issue
tracker prompt. The issue is a starting point for discussion, not a decision
record.

## Core Rule

Front-load alignment. First make sure the user can see what the issue entails
and agrees with the problem, goals, evidence, and decisions still open. Do not
jump directly from a pasted issue to an implementation plan.

The user approving execution with "do it", "go", or "approved" means "continue
the specifically requested next action." It does not mean every claim in the
issue or your response is now a hard requirement, and it does not imply
permission to implement a solution direction the user has not selected.

Ambiguous direction is not permission to decide. If the issue leaves the
problem, evidence, scope, requirements, technical direction, rollout path,
validation signal, or tradeoff unclear, present options and ask the user to
choose. Do not pick the path that seems most likely just to keep moving.

Prefer the smallest reversible solution that solves the evidenced problem.
Choose a narrow design that can be extended when a real need appears over a
supposedly bulletproof design that adds abstractions, schemas, modes, tooling,
or operational machinery for hypothetical cases. Treat rollback cost and every
new concept developers must preserve as immediate costs. Extensibility means a
clear path to add the next proven requirement, not implementing that future
requirement now.

## Immediate Response

When this skill triggers, do not edit files, write a plan, create commits, or
start implementing. Respond with an alignment brief:

```markdown
## My read of the task

- Problem:
- Goal:
- Non-goals or unclear scope:
- Evidence the issue provides:
- Evidence still missing:

## Assumptions to challenge

- ...

## Options I see

- Option:
- Current complexity and rollback cost:
- How it could extend later:
- Evidence that would support it:

## Decisions before planning

- ...

## Validation plan

### Automated tests

- ...

### Local validation

- ...

### Staging validation

- Exact supported steps:
- Expected result and signals:

### Production validation

- Exact supported steps or telemetry-only plan:
- Expected result and guardrails:

### Rejected validation paths

- ...

## Suggested next step

...
```

Keep it short enough for a real conversation. The goal is to give the user a
clean surface to correct and enough context to decide whether the work is worth
doing, not to bury them in analysis.

## Read The Issue Skeptically

Separate what the issue says into four buckets:

- Observed facts: concrete behavior, examples, logs, metrics, screenshots,
  customer reports, stack traces, or exact reproduction steps.
- Goals: what should be better after the work.
- Recommendations: proposed implementation, rollout, architecture, flags,
  tests, or sequencing.
- Open questions: anything needed to avoid solving the wrong problem.

Treat recommendations as hypotheses. Challenge them before adopting them. If
the issue says "we suspect", "probably", "should just", "recommended
approach", or "acceptance criteria" without evidence, call that out plainly.
For every recommendation, ask what would disprove it and what alternatives still
fit the observed facts. Do not turn the recommendation into the default plan
unless the user explicitly selects it. If evidence appears to rule out every
other option, present that evidence and ask for approval before planning around
the remaining path.

## Verify Before Planning

Before proposing a plan, identify what evidence would confirm the problem and
the right solution shape.

Prefer, in order:

- Telemetry: traces, metrics, logs, dashboards, alerts, job history, production
  counters, or timing data.
- Source truth: current code paths, call sites, existing configuration, tests,
  feature flags, schemas, API contracts, and deployment wiring.
- Product/user evidence: support examples, screenshots, reproduction steps, or
  concrete affected workflows.
- Historical context: prior issues, PRs, incidents, decision records, and
  Entire checkpoints when available.

Do not make the user wait for a full investigation before alignment, but be
clear about what should be verified before the work becomes a plan. If quick
read-only checks can answer a major assumption and the user's prompt permits
investigation, do those checks before presenting solutions.

If evidence is missing, leave the decision open. State what data would change
the recommendation instead of filling the gap with a plausible assumption.

## Define A Practical Validation Plan

Before planning, separate what can be proved cheaply in tests from what must be
observed in a running environment.

### Automated tests

List the behavior that is straightforward to cover at the smallest trustworthy
scope:

- Unit tests for pure decisions, validation, parsing, and state transitions.
- Integration tests for real wiring, databases, queues, configuration, process
  boundaries, and framework behavior.
- A small end-to-end or smoke test only when the critical behavior crosses the
  full system and lower layers cannot prove it.

Name the concrete success, edge, and error cases. Do not turn production-only
fault injection into a test seam or over-mock real boundaries.

### Local validation

Use local validation for scenarios that need synthetic bad data, database state
changes, queue-message injection, controlled failures, or unusual timing. These
are acceptable locally with fabricated data and existing development tooling.
State the exact command, fixture, setup, expected result, and cleanup. If new
tooling would be required solely for validation, call that cost out instead of
assuming it should be built.

### Staging and production validation

Use only supported, ordinary product or operator actions with safe synthetic or
internal data. For each environment, specify:

- Preconditions: deployment, flags, permissions, account/repository, and safe
  test data.
- Exact driver steps: CLI commands, API requests, or UI navigation and field
  values.
- Expected user-visible result and observable telemetry.
- Guardrails, rollback/failure signal, and cleanup.

Write executable instructions. If the driver is a CLI, include the exact
command with placeholders and required flags. If it is a UI, name the screens,
controls, values to enter, and action to click. If the exact interface is not
known yet, identify the source or `--help` output that must be inspected before
planning; do not replace it with a vague instruction such as "create a new
mirror" and do not invent a command.

Reject staging or production validation that requires intentionally malformed
data, manual database edits, handcrafted queue messages, ad hoc injection
tools, destructive state changes, or other unsupported manipulation. Move that
scenario to local automated/manual validation. If production cannot be driven
safely through a normal interface, say that direct production exercise is not
acceptable; use staging proof through a supported flow plus production rollout
telemetry and guardrails.

## Brainstorm Solutions Before Planning

Do not produce a step-by-step implementation plan until the user has aligned on
the problem and selected or approved a solution direction.

Discuss solution options at the level a manager would expect from a report
starting a project:

- What option solves the problem most directly?
- What current evidence pays for each new concept, abstraction, schema, mode,
  or tool?
- What does each option cost in complexity, rollback difficulty, rollout risk,
  operational risk, and future maintenance?
- Can the simplest option be extended later without implementing future cases
  today?
- What evidence would make this option clearly right or wrong?
- What is covered by tests, what needs local validation, and what supported
  staging or production steps prove the change works?
- What is the smallest reversible step?
- What could go wrong if the issue's recommendation is false?
- What should explicitly stay out of scope?

Prefer two or three real options, including "do nothing yet; gather evidence"
when the issue is weak. Do not invent filler options just to make the list feel
balanced. Do not select an option for the user. If evidence clearly eliminates
the others, label the remaining path as a recommendation, name the evidence that
makes it stronger, and ask the user to approve it before planning.

## Ask For The Right Approval

After the alignment brief, ask for the next decision. Good asks are specific:

- "Do you agree this is the problem worth solving?"
- "Should I verify the telemetry first, or should we inspect the code path?"
- "Which solution direction do you want me to plan around?"
- "Does this split between tests, local fault cases, and supported environment
  checks give enough confidence, or is a signal missing?"
- "Is this scope intentionally broader than the issue evidence supports?"

Bad asks are vague:

- "Does this look good?"
- "Should I proceed?"
- "Want me to implement?"

If the user approves only the next action, do only that next action. Do not
treat it as approval for every assumption, requirement, or implementation
choice in the issue or alignment brief.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Better |
| --- | --- |
| Turning the issue's recommended approach into the plan | Restate it as one hypothesis and ask what evidence supports it |
| Treating acceptance criteria as hard requirements | Ask whether the user agrees they are requirements |
| Starting implementation after "do it" | Use "do it" as approval for the alignment workflow unless the user explicitly selected a solution and asked for implementation |
| Choosing a technical direction because it seems obvious | Present the viable options, their costs, and the decision needed |
| Filling gaps with assumptions so planning can continue | Keep the gap visible and ask the user to resolve it |
| Producing a full plan before shared understanding | Present problem, goals, assumptions, decisions, and solution options first |
| Challenging the issue but still writing a plan | Stop at the decisions that need user agreement before planning |
| Designing for every hypothetical future case | Choose the smallest reversible solution and describe how it can extend when evidence appears |
| Treating tests as the only validation | Separate automated, local, staging, and production confidence |
| Writing "create a mirror" as validation | Give the exact supported CLI command or UI steps, or identify the interface evidence still needed |
| Mutating databases or injecting queue messages in staging/production | Exercise that failure locally with synthetic data; use supported environment flows and telemetry |
| Saying "done" after merge or deploy | Define the exact environment action and observable signal that prove the issue is fixed |
| Explaining basic engineering concepts | Assume a senior engineer; explain only local terms, ambiguous terminology, and hidden assumptions |

## Transition To Planning

Create an implementation plan only after the user has agreed on:

- The problem is worth solving.
- The goal and scope.
- The evidence needed before editing, or the reason evidence is not available.
- The chosen solution direction or the set of options to spike.
- The validation split: concrete automated tests, any local-only fault setup,
  exact supported staging/production steps, observable signals, and rejected
  unsafe or impractical environment manipulation.
- Any actual hard requirements the user explicitly approved.

When planning, label unapproved items as assumptions, suggestions, or open
questions. Never call them requirements unless the user explicitly made them
requirements.

---
name: using-entire
description: >
  Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical
  intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire
  skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
---

# Using Entire

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the
recorded intent, don't guess.**

Entire checkpoints capture the prompts, transcripts, and decisions behind every
agent-driven change. When you need to understand why code exists or how a module
evolved, look up the checkpoint history first. Only fall back to inference from
code structure when no history is available — and label that explicitly.

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

## Scenario Routing

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|
| Code block provenance | "why is this like this" / "wtf is going on" / "what happened at src/auth.ts:42" / "tell me why this changed" | `what-happened` |
| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |
| Recall a task playbook | "have we done this before" / "recall how we did X" / "how did we do this last time" | `recall` |
| Replay feature history | "replay <feature>" / "walk me through how X was built" / "show me the journey of Y" | `replay` |
| Teach a repo topic | "teach me <topic>" / "how does <topic> work in this repo" / "give me a lesson on X" | `teach` |
| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |
| Generate a dispatch / summary | "summarize recent work" / "generate a dispatch" / "what was accomplished this week" | run `entire dispatch` directly |
| Code review with intent context | "review these changes" / "review this branch" / "audit before merging" | `review` |
| Hand off to another agent | "hand off this session" / "continue in another agent" / "pick up the codex session" | `session-handoff` |
| Convert session to skill | "turn this into a skill" / "make a skill from this session" | `session-to-skill` |
| Link session to other repos | "link session to other repos" / "attach session to the foo repo" | `session-crosslink` |
| General exploration | "understand this module" / "explore how auth works" / "help me understand the codebase" | _(self — see below)_ |

If the scenario clearly maps to a sub-skill, delegate entirely to that skill's
workflow. Do not duplicate their steps here.

## General Exploration Flow

When no specific sub-skill fits — e.g. the user asks to "understand this
module" or "explore how auth works" — use this flow:

1. **Identify key files** in the target area (entry points, main types, core
   functions).

2. **Check for checkpoint coverage** on each key file:

```bash
git log --format='%H %s' -5 -- <file>
```

Look for `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailers in the commit bodies:

```bash
git log --format='%H %b' -5 -- <file> | grep -B1 'Entire-Checkpoint:'
```

3. **Read intent for covered commits** — extract the checkpoint ID from the
   trailer, then use JSON output for non-interactive consumption:

```bash
entire explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

If you only have a commit hash (not a checkpoint ID), use:

```bash
entire explain --commit <sha> --no-pager
```

4. **Synthesize**: combine the recorded intent (from checkpoints) with the
   current code structure to build a comprehensive understanding.

5. **Report** your findings, clearly distinguishing:
   - Facts backed by checkpoint transcripts (label as "recorded intent")
   - Observations inferred from code alone (label as "inferred from code")

## AI Agent Usage Notes

When running Entire commands from an agent subprocess:

- **Always pass `--json`** for commands that support it and might prompt
  interactively. `--json` implies non-interactive output.
- **Always pass `--no-pager`** to prevent pager activation in subprocess
  contexts.
- **Always specify `--checkpoint <id>` or `--commit <sha>`** for
  `entire explain` — without a locator, the command falls back to an
  interactive picker.

## When No Checkpoints Exist

If the target code predates Entire or has no checkpoint coverage:

1. Say explicitly: "No Entire checkpoint history is available for this code."
2. Proceed with standard code understanding (read source, check git log, trace
   call sites).
3. Label all explanations as "inferred from code — not backed by recorded
   intent."
4. If the user wants deeper history, suggest `search` with related keywords —
   there may be checkpoints on related work even if the specific file isn't
   directly covered.

## Transparency Principle

Always make it clear whether your answer comes from:

- **Checkpoint-backed history** — you read the actual session transcript and
  know the developer's stated intent
- **Code inference** — you analyzed the code structure and are reasoning about
  probable intent

Never present inferred intent as if it were recorded fact. The core value of
this workflow is that distinction.

## References

For a deeper understanding of Entire's capabilities beyond what the sub-skills
cover, consult these resources:

- **CLI help**: run `entire help` to see all available commands and flags
- **Documentation**: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt — AI-friendly
  documentation index following the [llms.txt standard](https://llmstxt.org),
  designed to be consumed directly by LLMs and coding agents

name: issue-alignment
description: >
  Use when the user pastes or paraphrases a Linear issue, ticket, task, bug,
  feature request, acceptance criteria, product spec, or issue-generated prompt
  that could lead to implementation. Also use when the prompt includes issue
  IDs, acceptance criteria, "recommended approach", "do it", "come up with a
  plan", asks to start work from a tracker item, or asks how to validate an
  issue is complete after deploy.
---

# Issue Alignment

Use this skill before planning or implementing work that starts from an issue
tracker prompt. The issue is a starting point for discussion, not a decision
record.

## Core Rule

Front-load alignment. First make sure the user can see what the issue entails
and agrees with the problem, goals, evidence, and decisions still open. Do not
jump directly from a pasted issue to an implementation plan.

The user approving execution with "do it", "go", or "approved" means "continue
the specifically requested next action." It does not mean every claim in the
issue or your response is now a hard requirement, and it does not imply
permission to implement a solution direction the user has not selected.

Ambiguous direction is not permission to decide. If the issue leaves the
problem, evidence, scope, requirements, technical direction, rollout path,
validation signal, or tradeoff unclear, present options and ask the user to
choose. Do not pick the path that seems most likely just to keep moving.

Prefer the smallest reversible solution that solves the evidenced problem.
Choose a narrow design that can be extended when a real need appears over a
supposedly bulletproof design that adds abstractions, schemas, modes, tooling,
or operational machinery for hypothetical cases. Treat rollback cost and every
new concept developers must preserve as immediate costs. Extensibility means a
clear path to add the next proven requirement, not implementing that future
requirement now.

## Immediate Response

When this skill triggers, do not edit files, write a plan, create commits, or
start implementing. Respond with an alignment brief:

```markdown
## My read of the task

- Problem:
- Goal:
- Non-goals or unclear scope:
- Evidence the issue provides:
- Evidence still missing:

## Assumptions to challenge

- ...

## Options I see

- Option:
- Current complexity and rollback cost:
- How it could extend later:
- Evidence that would support it:

## Decisions before planning

- ...

## Validation plan

### Automated tests

- ...

### Local validation

- ...

### Staging validation

- Exact supported steps:
- Expected result and signals:

### Production validation

- Exact supported steps or telemetry-only plan:
- Expected result and guardrails:

### Rejected validation paths

- ...

## Suggested next step

...
```

Keep it short enough for a real conversation. The goal is to give the user a
clean surface to correct and enough context to decide whether the work is worth
doing, not to bury them in analysis.

## Read The Issue Skeptically

Separate what the issue says into four buckets:

- Observed facts: concrete behavior, examples, logs, metrics, screenshots,
  customer reports, stack traces, or exact reproduction steps.
- Goals: what should be better after the work.
- Recommendations: proposed implementation, rollout, architecture, flags,
  tests, or sequencing.
- Open questions: anything needed to avoid solving the wrong problem.

Treat recommendations as hypotheses. Challenge them before adopting them. If
the issue says "we suspect", "probably", "should just", "recommended
approach", or "acceptance criteria" without evidence, call that out plainly.
For every recommendation, ask what would disprove it and what alternatives still
fit the observed facts. Do not turn the recommendation into the default plan
unless the user explicitly selects it. If evidence appears to rule out every
other option, present that evidence and ask for approval before planning around
the remaining path.

## Verify Before Planning

Before proposing a plan, identify what evidence would confirm the problem and
the right solution shape.

Prefer, in order:

- Telemetry: traces, metrics, logs, dashboards, alerts, job history, production
  counters, or timing data.
- Source truth: current code paths, call sites, existing configuration, tests,
  feature flags, schemas, API contracts, and deployment wiring.
- Product/user evidence: support examples, screenshots, reproduction steps, or
  concrete affected workflows.
- Historical context: prior issues, PRs, incidents, decision records, and
  Entire checkpoints when available.

Do not make the user wait for a full investigation before alignment, but be
clear about what should be verified before the work becomes a plan. If quick
read-only checks can answer a major assumption and the user's prompt permits
investigation, do those checks before presenting solutions.

If evidence is missing, leave the decision open. State what data would change
the recommendation instead of filling the gap with a plausible assumption.

## Define A Practical Validation Plan

Before planning, separate what can be proved cheaply in tests from what must be
observed in a running environment.

### Automated tests

List the behavior that is straightforward to cover at the smallest trustworthy
scope:

- Unit tests for pure decisions, validation, parsing, and state transitions.
- Integration tests for real wiring, databases, queues, configuration, process
  boundaries, and framework behavior.
- A small end-to-end or smoke test only when the critical behavior crosses the
  full system and lower layers cannot prove it.

Name the concrete success, edge, and error cases. Do not turn production-only
fault injection into a test seam or over-mock real boundaries.

### Local validation

Use local validation for scenarios that need synthetic bad data, database state
changes, queue-message injection, controlled failures, or unusual timing. These
are acceptable locally with fabricated data and existing development tooling.
State the exact command, fixture, setup, expected result, and cleanup. If new
tooling would be required solely for validation, call that cost out instead of
assuming it should be built.

### Staging and production validation

Use only supported, ordinary product or operator actions with safe synthetic or
internal data. For each environment, specify:

- Preconditions: deployment, flags, permissions, account/repository, and safe
  test data.
- Exact driver steps: CLI commands, API requests, or UI navigation and field
  values.
- Expected user-visible result and observable telemetry.
- Guardrails, rollback/failure signal, and cleanup.

Write executable instructions. If the driver is a CLI, include the exact
command with placeholders and required flags. If it is a UI, name the screens,
controls, values to enter, and action to click. If the exact interface is not
known yet, identify the source or `--help` output that must be inspected before
planning; do not replace it with a vague instruction such as "create a new
mirror" and do not invent a command.

Reject staging or production validation that requires intentionally malformed
data, manual database edits, handcrafted queue messages, ad hoc injection
tools, destructive state changes, or other unsupported manipulation. Move that
scenario to local automated/manual validation. If production cannot be driven
safely through a normal interface, say that direct production exercise is not
acceptable; use staging proof through a supported flow plus production rollout
telemetry and guardrails.

## Brainstorm Solutions Before Planning

Do not produce a step-by-step implementation plan until the user has aligned on
the problem and selected or approved a solution direction.

Discuss solution options at the level a manager would expect from a report
starting a project:

- What option solves the problem most directly?
- What current evidence pays for each new concept, abstraction, schema, mode,
  or tool?
- What does each option cost in complexity, rollback difficulty, rollout risk,
  operational risk, and future maintenance?
- Can the simplest option be extended later without implementing future cases
  today?
- What evidence would make this option clearly right or wrong?
- What is covered by tests, what needs local validation, and what supported
  staging or production steps prove the change works?
- What is the smallest reversible step?
- What could go wrong if the issue's recommendation is false?
- What should explicitly stay out of scope?

Prefer two or three real options, including "do nothing yet; gather evidence"
when the issue is weak. Do not invent filler options just to make the list feel
balanced. Do not select an option for the user. If evidence clearly eliminates
the others, label the remaining path as a recommendation, name the evidence that
makes it stronger, and ask the user to approve it before planning.

## Ask For The Right Approval

After the alignment brief, ask for the next decision. Good asks are specific:

- "Do you agree this is the problem worth solving?"
- "Should I verify the telemetry first, or should we inspect the code path?"
- "Which solution direction do you want me to plan around?"
- "Does this split between tests, local fault cases, and supported environment
  checks give enough confidence, or is a signal missing?"
- "Is this scope intentionally broader than the issue evidence supports?"

Bad asks are vague:

- "Does this look good?"
- "Should I proceed?"
- "Want me to implement?"

If the user approves only the next action, do only that next action. Do not
treat it as approval for every assumption, requirement, or implementation
choice in the issue or alignment brief.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Better |
| --- | --- |
| Turning the issue's recommended approach into the plan | Restate it as one hypothesis and ask what evidence supports it |
| Treating acceptance criteria as hard requirements | Ask whether the user agrees they are requirements |
| Starting implementation after "do it" | Use "do it" as approval for the alignment workflow unless the user explicitly selected a solution and asked for implementation |
| Choosing a technical direction because it seems obvious | Present the viable options, their costs, and the decision needed |
| Filling gaps with assumptions so planning can continue | Keep the gap visible and ask the user to resolve it |
| Producing a full plan before shared understanding | Present problem, goals, assumptions, decisions, and solution options first |
| Challenging the issue but still writing a plan | Stop at the decisions that need user agreement before planning |
| Designing for every hypothetical future case | Choose the smallest reversible solution and describe how it can extend when evidence appears |
| Treating tests as the only validation | Separate automated, local, staging, and production confidence |
| Writing "create a mirror" as validation | Give the exact supported CLI command or UI steps, or identify the interface evidence still needed |
| Mutating databases or injecting queue messages in staging/production | Exercise that failure locally with synthetic data; use supported environment flows and telemetry |
| Saying "done" after merge or deploy | Define the exact environment action and observable signal that prove the issue is fixed |
| Explaining basic engineering concepts | Assume a senior engineer; explain only local terms, ambiguous terminology, and hidden assumptions |

## Transition To Planning

Create an implementation plan only after the user has agreed on:

- The problem is worth solving.
- The goal and scope.
- The evidence needed before editing, or the reason evidence is not available.
- The chosen solution direction or the set of options to spike.
- The validation split: concrete automated tests, any local-only fault setup,
  exact supported staging/production steps, observable signals, and rejected
  unsafe or impractical environment manipulation.
- Any actual hard requirements the user explicitly approved.

When planning, label unapproved items as assumptions, suggestions, or open
questions. Never call them requirements unless the user explicitly made them
requirements.

item.stdout:
## Subagent dispatch requires multi-agent support

Add to your Codex config (`~/.codex/config.toml`):

```toml
[features]
multi_agent = true
```

This enables the multi-agent tools that skills like
`dispatching-parallel-agents` and `subagent-driven-development` use.
Which tools you get depends on the multi-agent version your model
preset selects (current presets run V2; older ones run V1). Trust your
actual tool list over any table — including this one — when they
disagree.

- **Spawning:** give children a clean context with
  `spawn_agent {fork_turns: "none"}`; the default `"all"` copies your
  entire transcript into the child. On Codex 0.145+, role files under
  `~/.codex/agents/` attach to isolated forks via `agent_type`.
  Full-history forks accept `model` and `reasoning_effort` overrides
  (only `agent_type` is refused there) — isolated forks are the SDD
  default for context hygiene, not because overrides require them.
- **Fix rounds:** resume the implementer with `followup_task` — it
  delivers your message, triggers a turn, and transparently reloads a
  child the harness evicted. Never dispatch a fresh implementer on the
  theory that a spawned agent cannot be messaged again; on V2 it
  always can.
- **Lifecycle:** V2 has no `close_agent`. Finished children are
  evicted automatically when slots are needed; leaving them unclosed
  costs nothing. Only V1 sessions have `close_agent` — there, close
  reviewers when their review returns, and close each implementer
  after its task's review passes.
- **Model names:** never copy a model name from a skill, table, or old
  session into `spawn_agent` without checking it against your current
  spawn allowlist — V2 accepts only V2-capable presets and hard-errors
  on the rest.

## Waiting on children

`wait_agent` is an event subscription, not a poll: a long wait wakes
the moment a child produces mailbox activity, with the same latency as
a short one. Short-timeout polling buys nothing and costs a tool call —
and a context rebill — per poll. In measured sessions, roughly
two-thirds of all wait calls were short polls that timed out.

- While you still have local work, do not wait at all. A completed
  child's final answer is pushed into your mailbox and arrives with
  your next turn.
- When you are genuinely idle with children outstanding, wait in
  bounded stretches: `wait_agent` with `timeout_ms` 300000-600000
  (5-10 minutes). After each stretch — wake or timeout — post one
  status line, run `list_agents`, and chase any child that finished
  without reporting. Never stack polls shorter than five minutes; the
  event subscription wakes a bounded stretch just as fast as a short
  one.
- Completion mail cannot wake an idle controller (it is delivered
  without triggering a turn); covering that idle window is
  `wait_agent`'s only job. A stretch that times out with no activity
  is your cue to reconcile, not to shorten the next stretch.

## Model routing on spawns

Every `spawn_agent` you issue — including when you are yourself a
spawned child running a fan-out — sets `model` AND `reasoning_effort`

name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
---

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

## Subagent dispatch requires multi-agent support

Add to your Codex config (`~/.codex/config.toml`):

```toml
[features]
multi_agent = true
```

This enables the multi-agent tools that skills like
`dispatching-parallel-agents` and `subagent-driven-development` use.
Which tools you get depends on the multi-agent version your model
preset selects (current presets run V2; older ones run V1). Trust your
actual tool list over any table — including this one — when they
disagree.

- **Spawning:** give children a clean context with
  `spawn_agent {fork_turns: "none"}`; the default `"all"` copies your
  entire transcript into the child. On Codex 0.145+, role files under
  `~/.codex/agents/` attach to isolated forks via `agent_type`.
  Full-history forks accept `model` and `reasoning_effort` overrides
  (only `agent_type` is refused there) — isolated forks are the SDD
  default for context hygiene, not because overrides require them.
- **Fix rounds:** resume the implementer with `followup_task` — it
  delivers your message, triggers a turn, and transparently reloads a
  child the harness evicted. Never dispatch a fresh implementer on the
  theory that a spawned agent cannot be messaged again; on V2 it
  always can.
- **Lifecycle:** V2 has no `close_agent`. Finished children are
  evicted automatically when slots are needed; leaving them unclosed
  costs nothing. Only V1 sessions have `close_agent` — there, close
  reviewers when their review returns, and close each implementer
  after its task's review passes.
- **Model names:** never copy a model name from a skill, table, or old
  session into `spawn_agent` without checking it against your current
  spawn allowlist — V2 accepts only V2-capable presets and hard-errors
  on the rest.

## Waiting on children

`wait_agent` is an event subscription, not a poll: a long wait wakes
the moment a child produces mailbox activity, with the same latency as
a short one. Short-timeout polling buys nothing and costs a tool call —
and a context rebill — per poll. In measured sessions, roughly
two-thirds of all wait calls were short polls that timed out.

- While you still have local work, do not wait at all. A completed
  child's final answer is pushed into your mailbox and arrives with
  your next turn.
- When you are genuinely idle with children outstanding, wait in
  bounded stretches: `wait_agent` with `timeout_ms` 300000-600000
  (5-10 minutes). After each stretch — wake or timeout — post one
  status line, run `list_agents`, and chase any child that finished
  without reporting. Never stack polls shorter than five minutes; the
  event subscription wakes a bounded stretch just as fast as a short
  one.
- Completion mail cannot wake an idle controller (it is delivered
  without triggering a turn); covering that idle window is
  `wait_agent`'s only job. A stretch that times out with no activity
  is your cue to reconcile, not to shorten the next stretch.

## Model routing on spawns

Every `spawn_agent` you issue — including when you are yourself a
spawned child running a fan-out — sets `model` AND `reasoning_effort`
explicitly, per the Model Selection rules of the skill you are
executing. Setting `model` alone is a trap: the child's effort
silently resets to that model's default, not to yours.

Ask your human partner to add a machine-level backstop to
`~/.codex/config.toml` so any spawn that slips through still routes to
a deliberate tier instead of silently inheriting the session's most
expensive model:

```toml
[agents]
default_subagent_model = "<a mid-tier model from your spawn allowlist>"
default_subagent_reasoning_effort = "medium"
```

## Environment Detection

Skills that create worktrees or finish branches should detect their
environment with read-only git commands before proceeding:

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)
```

- `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` → already in a linked worktree (skip creation)
- `BRANCH` empty → detached HEAD (cannot branch/push/PR from sandbox)

See `using-git-worktrees` Step 0 and `finishing-a-development-branch`
Step 1 for how each skill uses these signals.

## Codex App Finishing

When the sandbox blocks branch/push operations (detached HEAD in an
externally managed worktree), the agent commits all work and informs
the user to use the App's native controls:

- **"Create branch"** — names the branch, then commit/push/PR via App UI
- **"Hand off to local"** — transfers work to the user's local checkout

The agent can still run tests, stage files, and output suggested branch
names, commit messages, and PR descriptions for the user to copy.

Merge branch 'main' into fix/checkpoint-read-remotes
Composes this branch's read-candidate chain with the metadata-branch recovery
tier that landed on main in #1994. Both rewrote getSessionsBranchTree to fix the
same symptom — a committed checkpoint reading as "not found" while the data
exists elsewhere — from opposite ends: #1994 added a network tier (fetch the v1
branch from a dedicated checkpoint_remote when it is absent locally and origin
never received it), this branch added candidate breadth (resolve several trees,
select by requested checkpoint). Four files were unions of orthogonal additions
(MetadataBranchFetcher alongside ReadRemotes in OpenEnv/OpenOptions/GitStore and
both explain call sites). persistent.go needed a real composition, resolved as:

1. Ordering is local-then-network. resolveSessionsBranchTrees resolves every
   candidate ref locally (free reads), and only when none of them holds
   checkpoint data does tryFetchMetadataBranch run. Candidates first is not a
   preference: the fetch is the only tier that touches the network.

2. #1994's recovery trigger generalizes from one tree to the chain.
   anyTreeHasCheckpointData replaces treeHasCheckpointData at the call site,
   keeping the reason the trigger is "no data" rather than "no ref": a local
   orphan carrying only initialization artifacts makes a ref resolve and would
   otherwise mask the miss. tryFetchMetadataBranch's once-per-store latch is
   untouched and matters more here, since each entry now resolves N candidates.

3. Three helpers superseded by the candidate list are deleted, all with zero
   remaining callers: getFetchingTree (replaced by getCheckpointFetchingTree),
   and resolveSessionsBranchTree plus resolveSessionsBranchRef (the origin-only
   single-ref resolution). That also removes the last ReadBootstrappableFromOrigin
   use, completing this branch's rename to ReadBootstrappableFromRemote.

4. Both error contracts survive. getSessionsBranchTrees errors only when no tree
   resolved at all (this branch's shape); when trees resolved but none holds data
   and recovery failed, it returns them with a nil error so List still reads as
   empty offline instead of hard-failing on a transport error — the property
   5c1db66ae called out explicitly.

Verified on the merged tree: both sides' pinning tests pass —
REDACTED and the new
persistent_metadata_branch_fetch_test.go for #1994's recovery, and the
read-candidate and read-confinement suites for this branch's chain — plus
mise run lint clean and mise run test:ci green.

Reviewers: decisions 1-4 are judgment calls made across two authors' designs and
deserve a second pair of eyes, particularly 2 (the generalized trigger) and 4

c32e8f23055d2864e540260bd76f1332cc252179
perf(checkpoint): bound the read chain and stop re-electing per call
Fixes two costs this PR's read-candidate chain introduced, both measured
against origin/main with a PATH-shimmed git counting subprocesses.

Unbounded worst case. Per-candidate budgets replaced single shared ones —
a real fix, since one shared budget let a hung leader starve the legacy
origin tier — but nothing bounded the total, and these read paths have no
outer deadline: `entire resume` sets none and main() uses
context.WithCancel, not WithTimeout. fetchBlobsByHash lost the most: it
used to run inside one 2-minute budget that also covered its fallback
fetches, and per-target budgets left those fallbacks on the caller's
uncapped context, so a stalled hydration could spend per-target budgets
and then a fresh per-candidate metadata chain on top.

ReadChainBudget now wraps all three chains — checkpoint ref hydration, the
metadata branch chain, and blob hydration including its fallbacks — with
per-candidate budgets nested inside, so every candidate keeps its own
window while the total stays bounded.

Sized as an absolute 3 minutes rather than "n tiers x one full window".
The multiple is the trap: at 2 x ReadFetchTimeout with today's two tiers
the ceiling equals the loop's own worst case, so it cannot bind and buys
nothing, and blob hydration's fallbacks inherit an already-expired
context. An absolute ceiling binds for every chain of two or more
candidates, leaves a single-candidate chain untouched, and does not go
quietly wrong when a third tier appears. ReadChainLoopBudget holds back a
sixth of it so the fallbacks are funded rather than merely inside it, and
ReadFetchTimeout is exported so the cli-side paths stop carrying their own
2-minute literals that had to stay silently equal to it.

Election cost per command. The election re-runs on every call by design,
and each run shells out to git twice over .git/config: which remotes
exist, and does remote X exist. One command elects several times —
`entire checkpoint list` resolves the chain four times (disconnection
warning, branch listing, the git-refs store's remote discovery, imported
rewind points), spending 15 git subprocesses where main spent 9.

WithGitRemoteCache memoizes only those two .git/config reads, installed on
the root context in main(). The election result, settings, and the
captured-election file stay uncached, so a write followed by a re-resolve
still sees the new value — #1991's capture keeps working, which caching the
election result would have silently broken. Context-scoped and opt-in, so
an uninstrumented context behaves exactly as before and tests cannot leak
one temp repo's remote list into another.

Process scope is not invocation scope for every command: `entire mcp`
serves an agent session from one context, so it installs a fresh cache per
request via WithFreshGitRemoteCache rather than pinning one snapshot of
"which remotes exist" for hours. `entire repo mirror use` is the only
git-remote mutation in the CLI and invalidates after its writes.

WarnIfMetadataDisconnected now takes the caller's context instead of
building context.Background(): the detached context ignored both interrupt
cancellation and the cache, re-shelling out for answers the caller already
had.

Measured, `entire checkpoint list`: main 9 subprocesses, this PR before
these changes 15, after 9 — the regression is fully recovered (1 config
--get-regexp and 2 remote get-url, same as main).

Tests: the ceiling test stalls every target under a production-shaped
ratio (ceiling below targets x per-target, which is what makes it bind)
and asserts the call returns in ~ceiling — 0.58s with the ceiling, 1.09s
and failing without. Cache tests cover opt-in behavior, empty lists as
real answers, negative caching, invalidation, and an end-to-end guard that
a remote added mid-invocation is visible to a later election after
invalidation.

  avoid object transfer; pulling a whole v1 branch to render a list contradicts
  it. Naming a checkpoint is what earns the fetch.

  parses each time.

  the push path's budget is the constant's value rather than twice it.

  claim that v1 is still adopted from a checkpoint_remote this series made false.

06cf99433176046480dee697c72d592cf7158fb6
fix(explain): recover the v1 metadata branch from the checkpoint remote
A fresh clone of a repo whose checkpoints live on a dedicated
checkpoint_remote could not read any legacy hex-ID checkpoint. The
git-branch store resolved reads from the local v1 ref, then from origin's
remote-tracking ref, then gave up — and a checkpoint_remote setup has
neither, because the branch was never pushed to origin. `entire explain
<hex-id>` reported the checkpoint as unreadable with no way to recover.

Add a third tier: MetadataBranchFetchFunc, the git-branch counterpart to
the git-refs store's RefFetchFunc. Where that store resolves one missing
per-checkpoint ref, this one resolves the single branch the whole record
lives on. It is injected from the CLI layer like the other fetchers, so
the checkpoint package still resolves no remotes itself.

The tier is recovery, not refresh: it fires only when the branch resolves
neither locally nor from origin, so a normal read stays local and the hot
paths — which do not wire a fetcher at all — stay network-free. A failed
fetch leaves the original not-found error intact, keeping List's
offline-reads-as-empty behavior.

Wired into explain's read paths only. resume already self-heals through
its own fetch ladder; the remaining callers are hooks and background
paths where a network call on read would be wrong.

cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/remote_operation…2533 tokens truncated…t WithTimeout. fetchBlobsByHash lost the most: it
used to run inside one 2-minute budget that also covered its fallback
fetches, and per-target budgets left those fallbacks on the caller's
uncapped context, so a stalled hydration could spend per-target budgets
and then a fresh per-candidate metadata chain on top.

ReadChainBudget now wraps all three chains — checkpoint ref hydration, the
metadata branch chain, and blob hydration including its fallbacks — with
per-candidate budgets nested inside, so every candidate keeps its own
window while the total stays bounded.

Sized as an absolute 3 minutes rather than "n tiers x one full window".
The multiple is the trap: at 2 x ReadFetchTimeout with today's two tiers
the ceiling equals the loop's own worst case, so it cannot bind and buys
nothing, and blob hydration's fallbacks inherit an already-expired
context. An absolute ceiling binds for every chain of two or more
candidates, leaves a single-candidate chain untouched, and does not go
quietly wrong when a third tier appears. ReadChainLoopBudget holds back a
sixth of it so the fallbacks are funded rather than merely inside it, and
ReadFetchTimeout is exported so the cli-side paths stop carrying their own
2-minute literals that had to stay silently equal to it.

Election cost per command. The election re-runs on every call by design,
and each run shells out to git twice over .git/config: which remotes
exist, and does remote X exist. One command elects several times —
`entire checkpoint list` resolves the chain four times (disconnection
warning, branch listing, the git-refs store's remote discovery, imported
rewind points), spending 15 git subprocesses where main spent 9.

WithGitRemoteCache memoizes only those two .git/config reads, installed on
the root context in main(). The election result, settings, and the
captured-election file stay uncached, so a write followed by a re-resolve
still sees the new value — #1991's capture keeps working, which caching the
election result would have silently broken. Context-scoped and opt-in, so
an uninstrumented context behaves exactly as before and tests cannot leak
one temp repo's remote list into another.

Process scope is not invocation scope for every command: `entire mcp`
serves an agent session from one context, so it installs a fresh cache per
request via WithFreshGitRemoteCache rather than pinning one snapshot of
"which remotes exist" for hours. `entire repo mirror use` is the only
git-remote mutation in the CLI and invalidates after its writes.

WarnIfMetadataDisconnected now takes the caller's context instead of
building context.Background(): the detached context ignored both interrupt
cancellation and the cache, re-shelling out for answers the caller already
had.

Measured, `entire checkpoint list`: main 9 subprocesses, this PR before
these changes 15, after 9 — the regression is fully recovered (1 config
--get-regexp and 2 remote get-url, same as main).

Tests: the ceiling test stalls every target under a production-shaped
ratio (ceiling below targets x per-target, which is what makes it bind)
and asserts the call returns in ~ceiling — 0.58s with the ceiling, 1.09s
and failing without. Cache tests cover opt-in behavior, empty lists as
real answers, negative caching, invalidation, and an end-to-end guard that
a remote added mid-invocation is visible to a later election after
invalidation.

refactor: address cleanup review on the checkpoint fetch changes
Efficiency:
- Latch the metadata-branch recovery fetch to one attempt per store. A single
  command re-enters getSessionsBranchTree several times (List, then
  getFetchingTree per read), so an unrecoverable branch re-paid the whole fetch
  budget on every entry — multiplying one command's worst case by its read count,
  and amplified by the budget raise in the same series. Pinned by a new test.
- Drop MetadataBranchFetcher from getBranchCheckpoints. That is pure enumeration
  (`checkpoint list` / the branch explain view) and sits beside
  WithRemoteListDiscovery, which keeps the refs side to names-only precisely to
  avoid object transfer; pulling a whole v1 branch to render a list contradicts
  it. Naming a checkpoint is what earns the fetch.
- Resolve the git-refs decision once per path instead of per call site:
  pushSettings carries primaryIsRefs (prePush no longer re-reads the checkpoints
  config), and EnsurePrimaryRef passes its already-computed value into the
  bootstrap. LoadCheckpointsConfig is uncached — two whole-file reads and JSON
  parses each time.
- Share one deadline across the ls-remote probe and the fetch that follows it, so
  the push path's budget is the constant's value rather than twice it.

Simplification and reuse:
- Flatten the fetch-and-retry block; correct the skipEmptyOrphan comment, whose
  claim that v1 is still adopted from a checkpoint_remote this series made false.
- Collapse checkpointRemoteCurrentBranch/RevParse onto the general git helper,
  and parameterize the local-repo builder the blob-filter test had re-inlined.
- Use testutil.BranchExists and the existing runEntire spawn helper; drop two

06cf99433176046480dee697c72d592cf7158fb6
fix(explain): recover the v1 metadata branch from the checkpoint remote
A fresh clone of a repo whose checkpoints live on a dedicated
checkpoint_remote could not read any legacy hex-ID checkpoint. The
git-branch store resolved reads from the local v1 ref, then from origin's
remote-tracking ref, then gave up — and a checkpoint_remote setup has
neither, because the branch was never pushed to origin. `entire explain
<hex-id>` reported the checkpoint as unreadable with no way to recover.

Add a third tier: MetadataBranchFetchFunc, the git-branch counterpart to
the git-refs store's RefFetchFunc. Where that store resolves one missing
per-checkpoint ref, this one resolves the single branch the whole record
lives on. It is injected from the CLI layer like the other fetchers, so
the checkpoint package still resolves no remotes itself.

The tier is recovery, not refresh: it fires only when the branch resolves
neither locally nor from origin, so a normal read stays local and the hot
paths — which do not wire a fetcher at all — stay network-free. A failed
fetch leaves the original not-found error intact, keeping List's
offline-reads-as-empty behavior.

Wired into explain's read paths only. resume already self-heals through
its own fetch ladder; the remaining callers are hooks and background
paths where a network call on read would be wrong.

refactor(redact): inject the initialized logger via context instead of global probes
Replace the two pieces of global state this branch introduced with
explicit injection from the cobra entry point:

- logging.Init now returns a context carrying the logger it built
  (session-stamped), via new WithLogger/LoggerFromContext. The hook
  PersistentPreRunE paths SetContext the returned context, so every
  downstream handler receives a ready logger instead of relying on
  package state.
- logging.IsInitialized is deleted. EnsureRedactionConfigured now takes
  the caller's context and gates the load-time summary on
  LoggerFromContext != nil — the readiness decision is data the entry
  point put in the context, not a mutex probe of the global.
- redact.SetWarnFunc and the warn-func atomic are deleted. The redact
  package takes a *slog.Logger by injection (Logger fields on
  CustomRulesConfig/PIIConfig/OPFConfig, a parameter on LoadPacks);
  nil falls back to slog.Default(), preserving standalone behavior.

Non-hook entry points (import, enable, resume, attach, clean, explain,
investigate, trail refresh, checkpoint resume) propagate the returned
context so redaction diagnostics keep landing in .entire/logs/ wherever
logging was initialized. doctor intentionally stays uninitialized: its
diagnostics fall back to stderr, and the summary is skipped.

item.stdout:
645fb125275aa35e4f5bf3c805717ce8e8b32822
fix(cli): make explain work against checkpoint_remote with partial-clone

`entire explain <checkpoint-id>` failed with "no checkpoint or commit
found" when the metadata branch was on a configured `checkpoint_remote`
but blobs hadn't been fetched yet. Three coordinated fixes:

1. v1Store now has a blob fetcher configured (the piece resume already
   had via SetBlobFetcher). Without it, go-git's Tree.File() returns
   ErrFileNotFound on a missing blob, which ReadCommitted translates to
   ErrCheckpointNotFound — making it look like the checkpoint doesn't
   exist when really only the blob is absent.

2. FetchBlobs now uses `git fetch-pack` instead of porcelain
   `git fetch`. Porcelain enforces partial-clone integrity checks that
   reject blob-only responses with "did not send all necessary objects",
   so `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` always failed against GitHub for
   repos with filtered_fetches enabled. Plumbing skips those checks and
   just downloads the requested objects.

3. FetchingTree.File now tries `git cat-file` BEFORE the network fetch.
   In partial-clone repos a blob is commonly on disk but invisible to
   go-git's storer (filtered out, or in a packfile not in the cached
   index). Without the short-circuit, every File() burned a network
   round-trip on already-local data — which compounded into per-File
   25s SSH-handshake-and-rejection delays before this fix.

The matching empty-list fetch chain for explain now mirrors
resume.getMetadataTree (checkpoint_remote → treeless origin → full
origin), and a per-checkpoint PreFetch batches all subtree blobs in one
fetch-pack call. Cold runs are ~1-2s; warm runs are sub-second.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Remove unused resolver field and add batch blob prefetching

Replace the dead `*BlobResolver` field in FetchingTree with the underlying
`storer.EncodedObjectStorer`, removing a wasted heap allocation per instance.
Add PreFetch() method that recursively walks the tree, collects locally-missing
blob hashes, and batch-fetches them in a single network round-trip. Wire
PreFetch into all three resume flow call sites so metadata reads no longer
trigger N+1 separate `git fetch origin <hash>` subprocesses.

Signed-off-by: Paulo Gomes <paulo@entire.io>
Assisted-By: Assisted-by: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 413cf123213d

d051359d1e922b5db51bca6c26f5f9462daa725e
feat(cli): show spinner + info while explain fetches from remote

`entire explain <id>` against a treeless checkpoint metadata branch can
take 1-2 seconds for the fetch-pack round-trip. Previously the command
was silent during that window — easy to mistake for a hang.

Adds two visual indicators on stderr:

1. "Fetching checkpoint metadata from remote" — shown when the empty-
   matches path triggers `getMetadataTree` / `getV2MetadataTree`.

2. "Fetching N checkpoint blob(s) from remote" — shown when the
   pre-resolve prefetch detects N missing blobs in the cp subtree(s).

The spinner uses the same Braille frames as the activity TUI's
`spinner.Dot` so the visual matches across commands. When stderr is
not a terminal (CI, redirected output, agent subprocess), the spinner
is suppressed and the message is printed once with a trailing "..." —
non-interactive callers still see what's happening without ANSI noise.

`prefetchCheckpointBlobs` was restructured to count missing blobs
upfront (via the new exported `FetchingTree.CollectMissingBlobs`) so
the spinner only shows when network work is genuinely needed; warm runs
where everything is already local stay silent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: c3c1ad356bad

transparently fetches missing blobs when accessing treeless-cloned metadata.
Updates resume path to use the same fallback chain (treeless fetch → local →
full fetch → remote tree) for consistency.

fix(cli): make explain work against checkpoint_remote with partial-clone

`entire explain <checkpoint-id>` failed with "no checkpoint or commit
found" when the metadata branch was on a configured `checkpoint_remote`
but blobs hadn't been fetched yet. Three coordinated fixes:

1. v1Store now has a blob fetcher configured (the piece resume already
   had via SetBlobFetcher). Without it, go-git's Tree.File() returns
   ErrFileNotFound on a missing blob, which ReadCommitted translates to
   ErrCheckpointNotFound — making it look like the checkpoint doesn't
   exist when really only the blob is absent.

2. FetchBlobs now uses `git fetch-pack` instead of porcelain
   `git fetch`. Porcelain enforces partial-clone integrity checks that
   reject blob-only responses with "did not send all necessary objects",
   so `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` always failed against GitHub for
   repos with filtered_fetches enabled. Plumbing skips those checks and
   just downloads the requested objects.

3. FetchingTree.File now tries `git cat-file` BEFORE the network fetch.
   In partial-clone repos a blob is commonly on disk but invisible to
   go-git's storer (filtered out, or in a packfile not in the cached
   index). Without the short-circuit, every File() burned a network
   round-trip on already-local data — which compounded into per-File
   25s SSH-handshake-and-rejection delays before this fix.

The matching empty-list fetch chain for explain now mirrors
resume.getMetadataTree (checkpoint_remote → treeless origin → full
origin), and a per-checkpoint PreFetch batches all subtree blobs in one
fetch-pack call. Cold runs are ~1-2s; warm runs are sub-second.

d051359d1e922b5db51bca6c26f5f9462daa725e
feat(cli): show spinner + info while explain fetches from remote

`entire explain <id>` against a treeless checkpoint metadata branch can
take 1-2 seconds for the fetch-pack round-trip. Previously the command
was silent during that window — easy to mistake for a hang.

Adds two visual indicators on stderr:

1. "Fetching checkpoint metadata from remote" — shown when the empty-
   matches path triggers `getMetadataTree` / `getV2MetadataTree`.

2. "Fetching N checkpoint blob(s) from remote" — shown when the
   pre-resolve prefetch detects N missing blobs in the cp subtree(s).

The spinner uses the same Braille frames as the activity TUI's
`spinner.Dot` so the visual matches across commands. When stderr is
not a terminal (CI, redirected output, agent subprocess), the spinner
is suppressed and the message is printed once with a trailing "..." —
non-interactive callers still see what's happening without ANSI noise.

`prefetchCheckpointBlobs` was restructured to count missing blobs
upfront (via the new exported `FetchingTree.CollectMissingBlobs`) so
the spinner only shows when network work is genuinely needed; warm runs
where everything is already local stay silent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: c3c1ad356bad

645fb125275aa35e4f5bf3c805717ce8e8b32822
fix(cli): make explain work against checkpoint_remote with partial-clone

`entire explain <checkpoint-id>` failed with "no checkpoint or commit
found" when the metadata branch was on a configured `checkpoint_remote`
but blobs hadn't been fetched yet. Three coordinated fixes:

1. v1Store now has a blob fetcher configured (the piece resume already
   had via SetBlobFetcher). Without it, go-git's Tree.File() returns
   ErrFileNotFound on a missing blob, which ReadCommitted translates to
   ErrCheckpointNotFound — making it look like the checkpoint doesn't
   exist when really only the blob is absent.

2. FetchBlobs now uses `git fetch-pack` instead of porcelain
   `git fetch`. Porcelain enforces partial-clone integrity checks that
   reject blob-only responses with "did not send all necessary objects",
   so `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` always failed against GitHub for
   repos with filtered_fetches enabled. Plumbing skips those checks and
   just downloads the requested objects.

3. FetchingTree.File now tries `git cat-file` BEFORE the network fetch.
   In partial-clone repos a blob is commonly on disk but invisible to
   go-git's storer (filtered out, or in a packfile not in the cached
   index). Without the short-circuit, every File() burned a network
   round-trip on already-local data — which compounded into per-File
   25s SSH-handshake-and-rejection delays before this fix.

The matching empty-list fetch chain for explain now mirrors
resume.getMetadataTree (checkpoint_remote → treeless origin → full
origin), and a per-checkpoint PreFetch batches all subtree blobs in one
fetch-pack call. Cold runs are ~1-2s; warm runs are sub-second.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 74b3190b7dfb

3005c7a87933d0485c2c3ccac059840cd9efa3cb
Remove unused resolver field and add batch blob prefetching

Replace the dead `*BlobResolver` field in FetchingTree with the underlying
`storer.EncodedObjectStorer`, removing a wasted heap allocation per instance.
Add PreFetch() method that recursively walks the tree, collects locally-missing
blob hashes, and batch-fetches them in a single network round-trip. Wire
PreFetch into all three resume flow call sites so metadata reads no longer
trigger N+1 separate `git fetch origin <hash>` subprocesses.

Signed-off-by: Paulo Gomes <paulo@entire.io>
Assisted-By: Assisted-by: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: 413cf123213d

b92b37b3c7f336737f19fdd1e71636f052356b40
refactor: use FetchingTree for on-demand blob resolution in checkpoint reads

Replace direct getSessionsBranchTree() calls with getFetchingTree() which
transparently fetches missing blobs when accessing treeless-cloned metadata.
Updates resume path to use the same fallback chain (treeless fetch → local →
full fetch → remote tree) for consistency.
